span: The respondent-plaintiff failed to discharge the onus.
why: Court states the requirements for adverse possession and rejects the claim on facts; it does not deny that title can be acquired, so the stance is MIXED.

span: a Muslim divorced woman unable to maintain herself is entitled to claim maintenance under Section 125 Cr.P.C. even after the iddat period was over
why: Court recounts what Shah Bano held as background to the 1986 Act; it does not here adopt the rule or state its own holding on the divorced wife's entitlement.

span: she can take recourse under Section 125 of the CrPC or file a petition under the 2019 Act
why: Headnote holding that a divorced Muslim woman can still seek maintenance under s.125 CrPC; headnote confidence is capped.

span: a broad and expansive interpretation should be given to the term “wife” to include even those cases where a man and woman have been living together
why: Concerns whether a woman living with a man qualifies as a wife under s.125, not the divorced wife's entitlement.

span: This Court held that there is no conflict between the two provisions.
why: Describes Noor Saba Khatoon on the relation of s.125 and the 1986 Act, mainly concerning children's maintenance; it is background, and adoption by the current court is not shown.

span: The Magistrate does not become functus officio after passing an order under s.125
why: Headnote on the court's power to revive a s.125 application under s.362; it does not address whether a divorced wife is entitled to maintenance.

span: upheld the right of Muslim women, including divorced Muslim women to claim maintenance
why: Historical narration of Shah Bano, the 1986 Act and Danial Latifi in a different case about marriage equality; it is background and not a holding on s.125.
